guidance:
Use only Table 1 to define structure and values. Do not take data from narrative text or footnotes; you may read them only to understand layout.

1) Table title and scope
- Set `table_title` to the caption of Table 1, copied verbatim.
- Work only within the boundaries of Table 1; ignore other tables and figures.

2) Columns and headers
- Reconstruct the entire header region before creating any cells.
- Add every explicit data column header to `columns`. This includes each group, arm, timepoint, and any separate statistics columns (such as effect size or risk measures) that have their own header cell.
- For multi-level headers (a top header spanning several subheaders), treat only the lowest-level headers as data columns. Build each `column_label` by combining higher-level and leaf text into a single unique string (e.g., "Top: Leaf"). Do not add the top-level header alone as a separate column.
- If the leftmost label column has its own heading, include that heading in `columns`, but never create cells for it; its body entries are represented by `row_label` (and sometimes `row_group`).
- Every `column_label` used in `cells` must appear exactly once in `columns`. Do not invent total or combined columns unless they are printed as headers, and do not create slightly varied names for the same column.

3) Row_group vs. row_label (table body structure)
- Read down the first column and distinguish:
  • Section/category headings: visually distinct, often spanning multiple columns or followed by a block of related rows.
  • Data rows: aligned with numeric or textual values in data columns.
- Use each section or category heading as `row_group` for all immediately following data rows it governs. The specific descriptor on each data row becomes `row_label`.
- Rows that are not clearly under any heading use `row_group` = null.
- If a section heading itself has values in data columns on the same line, represent that line with `row_group` equal to the heading text and `row_label` = null.
- Do not swap roles: `row_group` is always the broader section; `row_label` is the individual item within that section. Do not treat an item name as a group or a group name as a row label.
- When the same heading or item text appears multiple times, reuse the exact string for consistency.

4) Creating cells and capturing values
- A cell corresponds to one non-empty intersection of a data row and a data column.
- For every visible value in the body of Table 1 (numbers, text, percentages, symbols), create exactly one cell object with fields: `row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`, `value`.
- Copy each `value` exactly as printed, preserving punctuation, spaces, parentheses, ranges, units, percent signs, plus/minus signs, and textual markers such as "N/A" or dashes when they appear as values.
- Treat printed zeros as real values and include them.
- Do not create cells for blank entries. Never infer, calculate, or move values between rows or columns.

5) Avoid missing, extra, and duplicate cells
- Work systematically row by row. For each data row, scan across all data columns and:
  • Add a cell for every non-empty entry.
  • Do not add cells where the table cell is blank.
- Do not create cells for pure header or section rows that show no data values.
- Do not add derived totals, summary statistics, or subgroup values that are not explicitly present as table entries.
- Each combination of (`row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`) must be unique; never emit more than one cell for the same position.

6) String consistency
- Use the table wording verbatim for `row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`, and `table_title`, preserving spelling, capitalization, spacing, and symbols.
- Ensure that every `column_label` appearing in `cells` matches exactly one entry in `columns`, and that identical section headings are written the same way across all related rows.

Apply these rules to any Table 1 layout to capture the full structure and all non-empty values without adding, omitting, or rearranging data.
